title: Customer-facing messaging draft — batching SLO tiers (Hosted API)
content:
Last updated: 2026-02-05 (Nikhil)

Purpose
- Draft customer-facing language for the new latency SLO tiers (fast / standard / cost-efficient) used by workload-aware batching defaults in Redwood Hosted API.
- Goal: make it easy for customers to choose the right trade-off without over-promising on absolute latency numbers or implying per-request guarantees.
- This doc is copy + FAQ + examples for docs, Console, and support macros.

Non-goals
- Detailed scheduler behavior, queueing heuristics, or knob-level tuning (keep in internal docs).
- Promising “X ms for every request” or guaranteeing throughput under unbounded concurrency.

Messaging principles (important)
1) Lead with the trade-off, not the implementation.
   - Customers care about predictable latency vs lower cost. Batching is a means.

2) Use “targets” and “designed for” language.
   - Avoid language that sounds like a contractual SLA unless it actually is.
   - Say: “designed to meet published p95/p99 targets under typical workloads” vs “guarantees”.

3) Be explicit about what influences latency.
   - Model, region, prompt length, output length, streaming vs non-streaming, and concurrency.

4) Provide a safe default + an easy escape hatch.
   - Customers should know what happens if they do nothing, and how to override per route.

5) Avoid implying data handling changes.
   - Tier selection changes runtime batching behavior only; it does not change logging/retention or how customer data is processed.


Tier names + short descriptions (customer copy)

A) One-liner (docs + Console)
- Fast: Lowest tail latency. Prioritizes responsiveness and stable streaming.
- Standard: Balanced latency and cost. Recommended for most production endpoints.
- Cost-efficient: Lowest $/token. Trades off tail latency for higher throughput via more aggressive batching.

B) Slightly longer (docs)
- Fast tier is tuned to keep p99 latency low and streaming token delivery smooth, even when concurrency is spiky.
- Standard tier targets a balanced latency profile while improving throughput and cost vs fast.
- Cost-efficient tier maximizes throughput and reduces per-token cost, but may increase queueing delay and tail latency—best for background or non-interactive workloads.

C) Important qualifier sentence (include near tier table)
- Actual latency depends on model, region, prompt/output size, and concurrency. Tier selection controls batching behavior and expected trade-offs; it does not guarantee a fixed latency for every request.


Suggested default behavior (Hosted API)
NOTE: confirm with runtime/platform before finalizing wording; this is how we should explain it.
- If you don’t specify a tier, Redwood selects a recommended tier automatically based on the endpoint defaults and workload signals (e.g., streaming vs non-streaming).
- You can pin a tier per route (recommended) and still allow Redwood to apply workload-aware batching within that tier.

Copy option 1 (simple)
“By default, Redwood uses the Standard tier. You can switch to Fast or Cost-efficient based on your latency and cost goals.”

Copy option 2 (more accurate, but more complex)
“By default, Redwood selects a recommended tier for your route. You can also pin Fast, Standard, or Cost-efficient explicitly.”

Open question (PM): which default are we actually shipping for Hosted API at launch? (Standard-only default is simpler; auto-tier selection is more powerful but requires tighter messaging and support readiness.)


Where this copy shows up
1) Public docs: “Batching defaults & SLO tiers” page
2) Console: route settings UI (tier dropdown + “recommended” badge)
3) API reference: request parameter/header docs
4) Release notes / changelog
5) Support macros: “How do I force fast tier for streaming?”


Docs / Console microcopy proposals

Tier selector label
- “Latency tier”
Tooltip (short)
- “Choose the latency/cost trade-off for this route. Redwood applies workload-aware batching within the selected tier.”

Recommended badge text
- “Recommended”
Helper text
- “Recommended based on your recent traffic (streaming, prompt lengths, and concurrency). You can override at any time.”

“Why this tier?” (Console drawer headline)
- “Why Redwood recommends Standard”
Body (example)
- “Your route is primarily non-streaming with mixed prompt lengths. Standard balances tail latency while enabling larger batches for better cost. If you need tighter p99 latency or smoother streaming, choose Fast.”

Note: reason codes are internal; we should translate to plain language categories (e.g., “streaming”, “high concurrency”, “long prompts”).


API reference copy (Hosted)

Parameter name (proposal)
- batching_tier: fast | standard | cost_efficient

Short description
- “Controls the latency/cost trade-off for Redwood’s batching behavior.”

Safety note
- “If omitted, Redwood uses your route’s configured tier (or the default tier for the endpoint).”


FAQ (customer-facing)

Q: What are latency tiers?
A: Latency tiers let you choose a trade-off between tail latency and cost. Redwood uses tier-specific batching profiles designed to meet published latency targets while improving throughput and $/token.

Q: Does choosing a tier change my model or output quality?
A: No. Tier selection changes how requests are batched and scheduled for execution. It does not change your model selection. (If you also enable optional model variants or quantization separately, those may have their own quality considerations.)

Q: Does tier selection affect logging, data retention, or security controls?
A: No. Tier selection only changes runtime behavior (batching/scheduling). Your data handling and logging settings are unchanged.

Q: Which tier should I use for streaming chat?
A: Fast tier is recommended for interactive, streaming chat and agent experiences where responsiveness matters. It is tuned to protect tail latency and keep streaming smooth.

Q: Which tier should I use for background jobs (summaries, tagging, offline enrichment)?
A: Cost-efficient tier is usually the best fit. It is tuned for throughput and lower $/token, with higher tolerance for queueing delay.

Q: What’s the difference between Standard and Cost-efficient?
A: Cost-efficient uses more aggressive batching, which can reduce per-token cost but may increase tail latency (especially under bursty concurrency). Standard is a safer default for most user-facing endpoints.

Q: If I choose Cost-efficient, will my requests be slower?
A: Often yes at the tail (p95/p99), especially during bursts, because the system waits longer to form larger batches. For workloads that don’t need interactive latency, the cost savings can be significant.

Q: Are the latency targets guaranteed?
A: Redwood publishes targets and monitors them, but actual latency varies with model, region, prompt/output sizes, and concurrency. For formal SLAs, talk to us about Dedicated capacity.

Q: Can I set different tiers for different endpoints?
A: Yes. Configure a tier per route so user-facing and background traffic can use different trade-offs.

Q: What happens if I don’t pick a tier?
A: Redwood will use the default tier for the endpoint (or the tier configured on the route). You can change it at any time without changing your model or API integration.

Q: What happens during overload?
A: Redwood applies backpressure and protective limits to keep the system stable. Fast tier prioritizes tail latency protection; Cost-efficient prioritizes throughput but will still enforce safeguards to prevent unbounded queue growth.

Q: Can I override batching settings directly instead of using tiers?
A: Most customers should use tiers. Advanced overrides are available for enterprise and Dedicated customers who need tighter control or have unique traffic patterns.


Examples (docs)

Example 1: Streaming chat, prioritize responsiveness
- Recommended: fast

cURL:
POST /v1/chat/completions
Header: X-Redwood-Batching-Tier: fast
Body: { "model": "…", "stream": true, … }

Python (SDK):
client.chat.completions.create(
  model="…",
  stream=True,
  batching_tier="fast",
  messages=[...],
)


Example 2: Non-streaming summarization, balanced default
- Recommended: standard

Python:
client.responses.create(
  model="…",
  input="Summarize the following…",
  batching_tier="standard",
)


Example 3: Offline enrichment job, minimize cost
- Recommended: cost_efficient

TypeScript:
await client.responses.create({
  model: "…",
  input: payload,
  batching_tier: "cost_efficient",
});


Support guidance snippets (internal-facing but reusable)

When a customer reports increased p95/p99 latency:
- Confirm tier in effect (route config vs request override).
- For interactive endpoints: suggest switching to fast.
- Ask about changes in concurrency or prompt/output lengths.
- Check region/model-specific incidents before suggesting permanent changes.

When a customer asks “why did it choose this tier?”
- Provide high-level explanation: streaming vs non-streaming, prompt length mix, and concurrency are common drivers.
- Avoid exposing internal reason code strings in customer communications; translate to the plain language categories.


Risks / wording pitfalls (things to avoid)
- Avoid: “Fast tier guarantees p99 under X ms.”
- Avoid: “Cost-efficient is always cheaper.” (It usually is per token, but workloads vary; plus customer’s overall cost depends on output lengths and caching hit rates.)
- Avoid: “No impact on latency.” (There will be differences; that’s the point.)
- Avoid: “Auto-tunes per customer in real time.” (Not in scope for initial release.)


Open questions (to resolve before public launch)
1) Default semantics for Hosted API: Standard-by-default vs auto-recommendation logic.
2) Final parameter naming in API/SDKs (batching_tier vs latency_tier). Docs should match SDK.
3) What do we commit to publicly regarding targets? (Link to tier definition page with caveats.)
4) How much of overload behavior do we describe? Minimal, but not misleading.


Next steps
- Review with SRE (Sean) for SLA/SLO wording and overload messaging.
- Review with Runtime (Sofia/Lena) for correctness of “how it works” statements.
- Hand off to Docs (Elliot/Wei) for incorporation into docs IA and FAQ.
- Align Console microcopy with DES-771 and ensure we have “recommended” + “why” text ready for first iteration.
